# SK2290 — Every call discards this `out` parameter's value

<!-- Generated from Rules/Rikarin.Skala.Rules.Metadata/rules.json. Do not edit. -->

A `private` method computes a value into an `out` parameter that every call site in the compilation writes to a discard, so the work behind it is dead.

| | |
|---|---|
| Category | Correctness |
| Default severity | suggestion |
| Scope | Compilation |
| Needs a compilation | yes |
| Fix | no |
| Language version floor | 7.0 |
| Since | 2.0 |

## Why

An `out` parameter is a second return value the callee is obliged to assign, and the body usually does real work to produce it — a lookup, a parse, a computed span. When *every* call site spells `out _`, that obligation is paid and the result is thrown away at every point in the program that could have read it, so the computation is dead across the whole call graph. ⚠ **This is the callee's finding, and it is a different fact from `SK6040`'s.** `SK6040` looks at one call site and says the *variable* declared there is never read; this looks at the declaration and says *no* caller anywhere reads the value. Neither implies the other, and only the second says the method's own body is computing something nobody wants — which is the difference between tidying a call and deleting a computation.

⚠ **`private` is not a taste; it is what makes the question decidable.** A `public` method's callers live in assemblies that do not exist yet, so "every caller discards it" is unanswerable — that is ReSharper's `.Global` half, and it is excluded rather than attempted ([#324](https://github.com/Rikarin/SKALA/issues/324)).

## Example

Instead of:

```csharp
static bool TryParseHeader(string line, out Header header) {
    header = Header.Parse(line);   // nobody reads this
    return line.Length > 0;
}

void Read(string line) {
    if (TryParseHeader(line, out _)) {
        Accept();
    }
}
```

Write:

```csharp
static bool IsHeader(string line) => line.Length > 0;

void Read(string line) {
    if (IsHeader(line)) {
        Accept();
    }
}
```

## When it does not fire

⚠ **Report-only, and the reason is that no mechanical edit is safe.** Removing an `out` parameter is three edits in three kinds of place at once — the declaration, every call site's argument list, and the body, whose assignments to the parameter become writes to nothing and whose supporting statements may or may not still be needed. `skala fix` applies a minimal text-edit list against one `SourceText`; this repair is a refactoring across files whose last step is a judgement about what in the body was only there to feed the parameter. docs/plan/08's bar is "a fix **or** a stated reason none is safe", and this is the stated reason.

⚠ **Only the discard form counts as "discarded", and that is a deliberate fraction.** A caller writing `out var x` and never reading `x` is `SK6040`'s finding at that call site; after `SK6040`'s fix the same call reads `out _` and this rule becomes reachable on the method. The two compose in that order on purpose — writing "declared but never read" a second time here would be the same analysis in two rules, disagreeing eventually. So a method whose call sites all write `out var unused` is **not** reported until `SK6040` has been applied. All three spellings — `out _`, `out var _` and `out int _` — are recognised, asked of the operation tree rather than of the syntax: `M(out _)` parses its `_` as an ordinary identifier and only the bound operation says it is a discard. ⚠ **The draft also unwrapped an `IDeclarationExpressionOperation` to find the discard inside `out var _`, and that arm was dead code.** The three spellings differ in syntax and are indistinguishable in the operation tree — all of them arrive as a bare `IDiscardOperation` — so sabotaging the unwrap left every fixture green, including the positive written specifically to reach it. It is gone, and `positive/an-explicitly-typed-discard.cs` stays as the pin on the behaviour.

⚠ **Zero call sites is a decline, not a finding, and it is the guard that separates a rule from a noise generator.** "Every caller discards it" is vacuously true of a method nobody calls, and without this the rule would fire on every uncalled `private` helper in every tree. An uncalled private member is a different finding with a different repair, and it is not this one.

⚠ **Any use of the method's name outside the callee position of an invocation withdraws the finding** — a method group conversion `Func<string, bool> f = TryParse;`, a `nameof`, a delegate creation, a conditional `?.` call. Through a delegate the arguments are invisible, so the set of call sites stops being complete, and the analysis's one claim is completeness. The name check is deliberately over-broad: it matches on the identifier text across the whole compilation, so an unrelated member with the same name silences the rule. That costs findings and never costs correctness. Both `IdentifierName` and `GenericName` are watched, because a generic method's method-group conversion spells `TryParse<int>` and an identifier-only sweep does not see it. A **dynamically dispatched** call is recorded the same way, from the operation tree: `d.TryGet(out x)` on a `dynamic` receiver compiles, is not an `IInvocationOperation`, and would otherwise be an invisible call site.

⚠ **`partial`, `extern` and explicit interface implementations are declined.** A `partial` method is two symbols for one method and either part may be generator-owned, so the report would land on a declaration the author does not edit; `extern` has no body to contain the dead work. `virtual`, `abstract` and `override` need **no** guard and are not guarded: at `private` accessibility all three are compile errors — `private virtual` and `private abstract` are **CS0621**, and `private override` is **CS0507** as well, verified by probe rather than assumed. An explicit interface implementation *is* reported by Roslyn as `Accessibility.Private`, and it is declined by name — but the decline is a stated gate rather than a load-bearing guard, because its callers reach it through the interface and it therefore has zero visible call sites, which the zero-call-site guard already refuses.

⚠ **`Deconstruct` is excluded by name.** A `private void Deconstruct(out …, out …)` is reachable from `var (a, b) = this;`, from `foreach` deconstruction and from a positional pattern, and none of those is an invocation — the call sites would be invisible while an explicit `Deconstruct(out _, out _)` in the same type made every *visible* one a discard. It is the one out-parameter protocol the language calls by name instead of by syntax, so excluding the name covers all three forms.

**Generated code is analysed rather than skipped**, at `GeneratedCodeAnalysisFlags.Analyze`: a call from a generated `partial` part is a call, and at `None` the syntax and operation actions never run on generated trees, so those call sites are invisible and the rule fires falsely. Roslyn still drops a diagnostic whose own location is generated, because `ReportDiagnostics` is not set.

⚠ **`scope: "Compilation"` makes the rule non-cacheable (`RuleInfo.IsCacheable` is false), and that price is the point.** A `private` member is callable from nested types, which are different `INamedTypeSymbol`s, so no per-type or per-file analysis can see every call site; only a compilation-wide collection with a compilation-end decision can. Without a project the rule does not run at all.

⚠ **A name mentioned anywhere in text a `#if` switched off withdraws the finding, and that guard is the corpus sweep's finding rather than a precaution.** The rule's one false positive over the three reference trees was `Newtonsoft.Json`'s `TryParseMicrosoftDate`: two call sites, one discarding `offset` and one reading it, and the reading one inside `#if HAVE_DATE_TIME_OFFSET`. The finding was true of the configuration compiled and false of the library's own build, and nothing in the operation tree could have seen it — disabled text is trivia, carrying no nodes, no operations and no symbols. The scan is word-level rather than parsed, because disabled text need not be valid C# and there is nothing to bind; it over-withdraws, silencing the rule for any method whose name appears even in a comment inside a disabled region, and that direction costs findings rather than correctness.

**Not covered:** local functions and non-`private` members of a `file`-scoped type, both of which are equally bounded and neither of which is a `MethodDeclarationSyntax` with `private` accessibility.
